text.p: Germany's Bayerische Vereinsbank AG said on Thursday it expected to post a good profit this year after its operating profit rose by a slightly below forecast 15.2 percent in the first half.
"(The bank) thus sees itself excellently equipped for the new dynamic from its planned fusion with Bayerische Hypotheken- und Wechsel-Bank," the bank said in a statement.

Vereinsbank, which on Monday announced plans to merge with Hypo-Bank in a mega-deal to create Germany's second-ranked commercial bank and Europe's largest property financer, reported operating profit after provisions of 765.7 million marks ($419.8 million) for the first six months.
Analysts had on average predicted an operating profit of 815 million marks, up 22.6 percent.
The bank's shares, which have surged massively in recent days, were trading down more than two percent at 109 marks early on Thursday.
Vereinsbank said it expected a "good result" for the full year. In 1996, the bank posted operating profit of 1.636 billion marks and net income of 869 million.

The Bavarian specialist in mortgage banking said its pure banking business contributed 277 million marks to operating profit in the first six months while mortgage business contributed 488.7 million marks.
Net interest income rose 7.9 percent to 2.5 billion marks, providing a key boost, the bank said.

The biggest rise was in interest income from mortgage lending, which rose 12.2 percent to 800 million marks as the volume of new lending for private homes rose 11 percent to 9.8 billion marks. Interest income from banking business rose six percent to 1.7 billion marks.

Commission income rose 19.9 percent to 697.8 million marks, the bank said, of which about half came from securities and fund business. It noted that its assets under management had grown by 16.2 percent to 67.5 billion marks.
Vereinsbank also reported a slight rise in income from own account trading to 197.2 million marks from 191.8 million.
The bank said it itself contributed 68 percent of the result while its northern German subsidiary Vereins und West-Bank contributed 25 percent.
Risk provisions rose 13.1 percent to 498.5 million marks.
Spending rose by nearly eight percent to 2.1 billion marks, reflecting costs associated with efforts to improve company management and risk controls to create a basis for higher profitability.

Group staff levels fell slightly to 21,482 from 21,825 at the end of 1996, but Vereinsbank said this was mainly due to the ending of training periods and that it planned to take on 450 more trainees in the third quarter.
